name: Chloe Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing speech and language therapy, so it's phonetics, child development and a clinic observation day every other week. I live in a shared house with five people from different courses, and I work mornings at a café three days a week, making flat whites and doing the Instagram posts. My mum raised me alone and she's a dental receptionist, so she covers my rent top-up and I do the rest. I use AI to turn lecture recordings into notes and to quiz me, and I honestly can't imagine studying without it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, and I'd be a bit relieved. I'd tell my housemates the tools are already good enough for what I need. I'd also say nobody should plan their life around a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine with me. My course is mostly people work, so a plateau doesn't threaten it. What I do worry about is Mum, because the dental practice already uses a booking system that does half her job. Slow change would still be gradual change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on using the tools for study and keep the café job. I'd put 30 a week away, which is about what's left after rent. I'd try to get a volunteering spot at a children's centre, which is also what universities like to see. And I'd keep an eye on how clinics use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Relaxed, a little bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum's job is the bit I'd worry about. If the practice cut her hours by a day, her wage would fall by about a fifth. That's what pays for my top-up, so I'd go from three café mornings to four and probably sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in a school or a children's clinic, working one on one with a small child. I want to be there the moment a boy who can't say his 's' sounds says 'sun' for the first time. Speech therapists are always short, so I think I'll get a job.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful**, but nobody should plan their life around a promise.
I'd tell housemates my course is mostly **people work**.
think: A plateau doesn't threaten my course, but **Mum's** receptionist job is already shrinking.
Speech therapists are always **short**, so I expect to find a job.
do: Keep the **café** job and use the tools for study.
Get a volunteering spot at a **children's centre**.
S0.quote: I want to be there the moment a boy who can't say his 's' sounds says 'sun' for the first time.
fieldNote: Chloe feels **secure** because her field is people work and short of staff.
Her one pressure is **Mum's** hours at the dental practice.
She uses tools every day and sees nothing threatening in a plateau.

steps.text: Keep working three mornings a week at the café

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one that's already starting to show. I'd tell friends to learn the tools properly, not just copy and paste. And I'd say don't be scared, because people who understand the tools will be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is hands-on and people-heavy, but the notes, reports and booking would go to software. That's good, because therapists spend hours on admin. The worry is the clinics using it to cut therapist numbers. My mum's job, answering calls and booking, would go for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with the tools. I'd learn how to use speech software that gives children feedback, so I could be the therapist who's good at it. I'd pick a dissertation about tools in therapy. I'd also help Mum learn a new skill, like practice administration or clinic coordination, before the practice decides for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Positive, with a bit of worry for Mum. I like being on the early side of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The café would go first, since the owner's trying an ordering app and a coffee robot at the other branch. The Instagram work I do could be done by a tool too. Either could cut my mornings. I'd lose maybe six hours a week, but I could cover it with tutoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would change how, not what. I'd learn the speech tools alongside the therapy, and I'd practise checking what the tools say. A tool can listen to a child, but it can't tell that the child is frightened and about to give up.

say: I'd tell friends to learn the **tools** properly, not just copy and paste.
I'd say people who understand the tools will be **okay**.
think: Notes and booking move to software, which is good, but clinics might use it to **cut** therapists.
**Mum's** job answering calls and booking would go.

Pick a **dissertation** about tools in therapy.
Help Mum learn **clinic coordination** before the practice decides for her.

fieldNote: Chloe sees the tools as a **career edge**.

She names a concrete café risk of about six hours.

steps.text: Learn the speech feedback software for children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and we need rules fast. I'd say people should stay calm and stay curious, but not pretend it's fine. I'd also tell people not to wait for someone else to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be unsettled. Mum's job goes for sure, and I'm not sure how long the practice could afford me studying. Speech therapy is people work, so I think it lasts a lot longer, but clinics might not have the money to hire. Two years is just too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Mum right away and make a plan for her next job and for money. I'd keep the café and use the tools to earn: tutoring, content for small businesses, anything. I'd talk to my tutors about what hiring looks like in three years. And I'd focus on being someone a clinic can't do without, like the best at using tools with children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled, but I wouldn't freeze. I'd feel the pressure, and I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending to rent and food, and live more simply. I'd ask Mum to stop topping up if her hours go. I'd apply for hardship funds early, before everyone else does. And I'd look at whether I should do a placement year to get paid experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on Mum, my housemates, and a couple of lecturers who are honest. I'd use the tools for tutoring income. And I'd lean on a children's centre where I volunteer, to see what's really happening in clinics.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and need rules fast, but people should stay curious.
I'd tell people not to wait for someone else to **sort it out**.
think: **Mum's** job goes for sure, and I'm unsure the practice could afford my study.
Speech therapy is people work, but clinics might not have the **money** to hire.
do: Sit down with **Mum** and plan her next job and our money.
Earn from **tutoring** and content for small businesses.
S2.quote: I'd focus on being someone a clinic can't do without, like the best at using tools with children.
fieldNote: Chloe's anxiety is about **Mum's** income and clinic budgets, not her skills.
She turns pressure into **action**: income, funds, specialism.
She asks about a **placement year** for paid experience.

steps.text: Sit down with Mum to plan her next job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to be smart. I'd tell people to learn the tools, find a skill that's human, and look out for each other. And I'd say don't cut yourself off from news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit uneasy but fine. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years of work before the AGI date. Speech therapy is hands-on and human, so I'd have longer. I'd worry about the budget side and about Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and get clinic experience in every holiday. I'd save about 40 a week from the café and tutoring. I'd keep learning the tools and I'd get good at explaining them to others, because that's a skill. And I'd help Mum switch to a better-protected role in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. A five-year warning feels like enough time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I could do all of it in order, and with two I'd be scrambling for money and for Mum. I'd finish my degree and build a cushion, so a hiring freeze wouldn't wreck me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide at the end of second year. If clinics are growing, I'd stay on the course. If they're freezing hiring, I'd consider an extra qualification in something like special education, where a person's presence matters.

say: I'd say five years is enough to be **smart**, so learn the tools and a human skill.
I'd tell people to **look out** for each other.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with two **working years** before AGI, and hands-on therapy would last longer.
I'd worry about clinic **budgets** and about Mum.
do: Save about **40 a week** from the café and tutoring.
Help Mum move to a better-**protected** role.
feel: **Calm-ish**, because five years feels like enough to adjust.
S3.quote: With five years I could do all of it in order, and with two I'd be scrambling for money and for Mum.
fieldNote: The **warning time** is what calms Chloe.
Her decision point is the end of **second year**.
She treats explaining tools to others as a **skill**.

steps.text: Get clinic experience in every holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and I'd use it. I'd say learn how to learn, and keep up with the tools. I'd tell people to build savings and a skill nobody can copy cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pretty calm. I'd be 29, nearly seven years into a speech therapy career. Robots for hands-on work arrive about 2039. I'd have a decent run, and probably a senior role by then. I'd also be able to help Mum retire properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work in a clinic, and keep learning the tools. I'd save for a deposit on a flat. I'd also try something on the side, like an app or a resource pack for parents. And I'd keep building a network of other therapists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. This is the one that feels like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me build a career, help Mum, and try side projects. Two years would just be a scramble. I think the ten-year picture is where people with a plan do best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to do it, because people always need to be heard and understood. I'd say learn the tools in first year and don't wait until you think you need them. Choosing work that needs a human is a smart bet, not a risk.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, so learn how to learn and keep up with the tools.
I'd tell people to build **savings** and a skill nobody can copy cheaply.
think: I'd be 29, nearly seven years into **therapy work**, probably in a senior role.
I'd be able to help **Mum** retire properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my mum's job would go before she could prepare and I'd be juggling study and money. What would help is time to retrain Mum, hardship funds for students, and a university that tells us honestly what clinics are hiring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that my generation isn't scared of tools, we're scared of what happens to our parents. A lot of us are thinking about our mums and dads as much as ourselves.

headlineQuote: My generation isn't scared of tools, we're scared of what happens to our parents.
portrait: Chloe is a **speech and language therapy** first-year, 19, in a shared house with five others.
Her mum raised her alone and works as a **dental receptionist**, which is where Chloe's worry sits.
She is centrist and adaptive, uses AI tools **every day** and treats them as a career edge.
She works at a café and tutors, and she turns pressure into **action** quickly.
Her mood is calm in slower worlds and anxious when AGI is two years away because of **Mum's job**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because Mum's job would go before she could prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Time and funds to **retrain** Mum, student hardship funds and honest information on clinic hiring.
